items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: World Food Programme sets out 2027 plan to assist 91 million people in need as food crisis looms
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: World
Source: World Food Programme

ROME – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) today launched its Global Outlook for 2027, outlining its plans to assist 91 million people in need next year at a cost of just over USD12 billion.

The number of people WFP will support, however, does not represent the full scale of global hunger, with as many as 266 million people facing acute hunger in 2025, according to the Global Report on Food Crises (GRFC), and an estimated 39 million at emergency levels or worse.

Amidst this challenging global context and warnings that the world could face its third major global food crisis in six years, WFP is pivoting its focus to efficiencies that will extend the agency’s reach to the most vulnerable. This includes scaling anticipatory action initiatives, including the provision of insurance and pre-arranged finance that will enable communities to better prepare ahead of climatic shocks. WFP will also scale up use of local partners and expand market-based assistance to help extend limited resources more effectively.

“For the world’s most vulnerable people, acute hunger is becoming harder to escape,” said WFP Executive Director Luke J. Lindberg. “We can protect the most vulnerable, but it will require sustained political commitment, investment and collective action. I urge others to join our call and take action to ensure no more famines, no more weaponization of food, and no more attacks on humanitarians.”

Nearly 72 percent of WFP’s requirements for 2027 are for crisis response, while 28 percent supports resilience-building. Every contribution made to WFP helps saves lives today while creating the conditions for communities to become more resilient tomorrow.

# # #

The WFP 2027 Global Outlook can be accessed here.

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: UNHCR CAR Operational Update September
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Countries: Central African Republic, Sudan
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

UNHCR's operations in the Central African Republic (CAR) are built on protection through presence, the cornerstone of the humanitarian response. Amid volatile security conditions and the spillover of the crisis in Sudan, UNHCR also remains ready to respond to emergencies. Durable solutions are another top priority supporting the voluntary, safe, and dignified return of Central African refugees, their sustainable reintegration, and their contribution to national development. Together with the Government of CAR and its partners, UNHCR provides protection and multisectoral assistance to internally displaced people (IDPs) and refugees, including Sudanese and Chadian refugees, while promoting durable solutions for Central Africans returning home. Its work is aligned with national priorities: the National Development Plan, the National Strategy for Durable Solutions and the Solutions Support Platform established under the 2022 Yaoundé Declaration.

items.creator: UN Children's Fund
items.title: Child casualties in Ukraine reach highest level in almost four years – UNICEF
items.author: UN Children's Fund
items.content:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN Children's Fund

As families prepare to face winter, verified attacks on energy infrastructure have reached unprecedented levels since the start of the full-scale war

KYIV, 20 November 2026 – At least 1,144 children have been killed or injured in Ukraine in the first ten months of 2026, a higher number of verified child casualties than in any of the past three years. According to the Human Rights Monitoring Mission for Ukraine (HRMMU), at least 114 children have been killed and 1,030 injured between January and October this year. That is an average of more than three children killed or injured every single day. Overnight, large-scale attacks were reported in Kyiv and several other parts of the country, killing and injuring civilians as well as damaging critical infrastructure.

Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, a 150 per cent increase when compared to the same period last year. These latest figures reflect an alarming escalation in violence affecting children in Ukraine. Attacks involving missiles and armed drones continue to put children and families at risk in their homes, schools, and communities, including far from the frontline.

With two months remaining in the year, the number of children killed in Ukraine in 2026 has already exceeded the total for 2025 by more than 20 per cent, while the number of children injured has risen by almost 60 per cent.

“Children have been paying an unacceptable price for this war for too long. Every child killed is a life and future lost, and every child injured may face lasting physical and psychological consequences. Children must be protected, wherever they are,” said UNICEF Representative in Ukraine, Anne-Claire Dufay. “Today is World Children’s Day, when we should be celebrating children’s rights. But in Ukraine they continue to live in fear in their homes, neighborhoods, and places where they should feel safe.”

Deadly attacks against civilians have indeed continued into this month. On 2 November, a strike on a school compound in Southeastern Ukraine, including an underground shelter where humanitarian assistance was being distributed, reportedly killed 72 people, with four others still missing. On 13 November, a 17-year-old boy was reportedly killed and eight other children injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia city, underscoring the continued threat to children’s lives and safety.

In addition, verified attacks on energy infrastructure in 2026 are at their highest level since the start of the full-scale war, with 78 per cent more attacks already verified than in all of 2025. Scheduled outages are now in force across most regions, lasting between 4 and 18 hours, with power cuts exceeding 12 hours in early November, as heating and power plants continue to be heavily damaged.

When power is cut, water supplies to homes, schools, and health facilities can also be disrupted, leaving children without safe water for drinking and hygiene and increasing the risk of disease. Last winter, nearly two million children were left without heat, electricity, and water as temperatures fell below minus 20°C.

UNICEF is supporting district energy projects to maintain heating for around three million people in the hardest-hit municipalities. With partners, UNICEF is installing alternative power sources in health facilities to keep essential maternal and child health services running, and solar power at critical water supply sites serving around 2.5 million people.

With the Ministry of Social Policy, UNICEF is also providing winter cash assistance to more than 100,000 households in frontline regions. UNICEF and partners are also repairing damaged education facilities, rehabilitating school shelters, and providing learning, mental health, and psychosocial support to children, young people, and families.

Despite all efforts, too many children in Ukraine continue to be at the sharp end of unrelenting war. UNICEF calls for the protection of civilians, including children, and the infrastructure they depend on, including energy, heating, and water systems, in accordance with international humanitarian law. Safe and unimpeded humanitarian access across Ukraine, including occupied territories, remains critical.

items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: WFP Lebanon Country Brief, November 2026
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Countries: Lebanon, Syrian Arab Republic
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• As needs continue to outpace initial planning assumptions, WFP requires immediate, flexible, and front-loaded funding at scale to sustain and expand assistance in a highly fluid operational environment.

• Since the beginning of the escalation on 2 March, WFP has reached around 1.1 million unique conflict‑affected people with food and cash assistance in shelters and across communities.

• In October, the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE), with WFP and UNICEF, launched Lebanon’s first National Nutrition and Food Environment Report, with findings establishing a national baseline and providing evidence to inform policies and programmes.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Lebanon's political and security environment remains fragile, amid unresolved conflict with Israel. Persistent Israeli military operations across southern Lebanon have caused civilian casualties, infrastructure damage, and disruption to livelihoods and essential services. Since the renewed escalation on 2 March 2026, Israeli military operations have resulted in 4,389 deaths and more than 12,424 injuries as of end-October 2026.

• Despite increasing returns, Lebanon’s humanitarian situation remains critical. By end of October, 965,000 people had returned to their area of origin of whom 27 percent are still locally displaced within their governorate. Meanwhile, over 304,000 remained displaced and 11,200 stayed in shelters.

• The September 2026 Integrated Food Security Phase classification (IPC) analysis shows that 1.05 million people (21 percent of the analysed population) are experiencing acute food insecurity, with conditions projected to deteriorate further in 2027. Lebanese residents account for the largest share of the affected population, representing 65 percent (686,000 people) of those acute food insecure. Conflict-affected areas, in southern Lebanon, continue to face significant food security pressures. The situation is primarily driven by persistent economic hardship, high living costs, limited employment, and localized insecurity.

• The conflict has severely disrupted education, with 86 teachers killed or injured and 436 education facilities affected as of end of October 2026. Additionally, 101 schools were damaged or destroyed, while 57 public schools remain occupied as collective shelters, limiting access to education.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: South Sudan Situation: UNHCR External Update #14 - September 2026
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Countries: South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

▪ South Sudan: Conflict across Jonglei and Upper Nile States continued to drive displacement, with more than 440,000 people displaced since January 2026 and Northern Jonglei at the centre of the crisis. Meanwhile, spontaneous returns from Ethiopia increased amid localized security improvements. In Eastern Equatoria, drought resulted in crop failures, water shortages, livestock losses and severe malnutrition.

▪ Ethiopia: In Gambella, insecurity intensified in September, resulting in deaths, injuries and localized displacement, including attacks on a public convoy and clashes near the UNHCR compound. Movement restrictions and the suspension of convoys along the Itang corridor from 28 September disrupted food distributions, water supplies and medical referrals.

items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: WFP Djibouti Country Brief November 2026
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: Djibouti
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

  • WFP prepared to transition all Markazi refugees to cash-based assistance from November, following the emergency response to arrivals from Yemen in Obock. Support included 72,690 hot meals between 11 September and 7 October and 8,000 fortified biscuit rations; hot meals ended on 7 October after newly arrived families received tents and cooking utensils.
  • In October, WFP dispatched 23 MT of food for the refugee response and transferred approximately USD 49,722 through cashbased activities supporting fresh-food voucher and school-garden interventions.
  • WFP strengthened anticipatory action and preparedness through regional dialogue and local technical engagement, including an ECHO technical mission to Tadjourah and Obock from 6 to 8 October.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: South Sudan Situation: UNHCR External Update #13 - August 2026
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Countries: South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

▪ South Sudan: Conflict across Jonglei and Upper Nile States has displaced more than 323,000 people since January 2026, with Northern Jonglei at the epicenter of the current crisis. At the same time, UNHCR is preparing for climate shoks due to El Nino, including localized flooding, worsening food insecurity and disruptions of livelihood and humanitarian actions.

▪ Ethiopia: The environment remained volatile in the Gambella region, throughout August, with localized security incidents affecting security and humanitarian access. On 23 August, an armed attack on a public bus along the Itang corridor killed one person and injured 15 others, resulting in the cancellation of a humanitarian convoy. Meanwhile, expanding military operations in parts of Jonglei and Upper Nile continued to drive displacement into Ethiopia.

▪ Uganda: On 19 August, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) reinstated prima facie refugee status for asylum-seekers from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), South Sudan and Sudan, following a review of conditions in the three countries. The directive took immediate effect and also granted refugee status to individuals from these countries whose claims were undergoing individual Refugee Status Determination.

items.creator: CCCM Cluster
items.title: Chad : Humanitarian Situation in Lac Situation Report N° 02 (30 October 2026)
items.author: CCCM Cluster
items.content:
Country: Chad
Sources: CCCM Cluster, Education Cluster, Food Security Cluster, Government of Chad, Health Cluster, International Organization for Migration, Nutrition Cluster, Protection Cluster, Shelter Cluster, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, WASH Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

This report was produced by OCHA in collaboration with the authorities and humanitarian partners. It primarily covers the period from 1 to 30 October 2026 and incorporates findings from the July 2026 mid-term evaluation of the response to internally displaced persons (IDPs). The next report will be published at the end of November 2026.

KEY POINTS

  • 307,206 displaced people in the province according to IOM Round 26, including 268,064 IDPs, 17,100 returnees, and 22,042 former IDPs who have returned.
  • More than 75,000 IDPs have been hosted across 16 sites in the Fouli and Kaya departments since May 2026. New population movements continue to be reported and remain under verification.
  • An encouraging improvement in the cholera situation was observed between 13 and 26 October, followed by a resurgence of 12 new cases in Kiskawa. However, the case fatality rate remains high (5.78%), well above the WHO emergency threshold, requiring the need to strengthen prevention, surveillance, and WASH interventions.
  • The areas of Liwa, Kiskawa, Kadoulou, and Daboua are among those most exposed to security risks. This insecurity directly contributes to population displacement, loss of livelihoods, and reduced access to basic services.
  • Four incidents were reported in the departments of Fouli and Kaya, affecting several civilians and resulting in dozens of deaths as well as abductions, a toll that would have been even higher without the intervention of the defense and security forces.
  • Despite the scale of needs, the protection sector remains the least covered, with only 0.3% of targeted people assisted.
  • A concerning deterioration in livelihoods has been observed linked to low rainfall.
  • US$10.6 million has been mobilized through humanitarian emergency funding mechanisms, including CERF, the Regional Humanitarian Fund, and anticipatory action, to support the response.
  • Significant humanitarian needs remain unmet due to insufficient funding, particularly in protection, shelter and site management, education, health and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
  • The revitalization of the Grand Cadre Nexus and the review of convergence zones offer an opportunity to strengthen integrated investments by linking emergency response, access to essential services, social cohesion, and resilience.

items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: UNHAS South Sudan - Concept of Operations
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: South Sudan
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Aviation a critical enabler of humanitarian response in South Sudan, particularly for remote and hard-to-reach communities. In this context, UNHAS South Sudan serves approximately 48 destinations, transports more than 4,000 passengers each month, and supports around 200 humanitarian organizations through a fleet of 10 aircraft.

More than 50 percent of destinations are accessible only byhelicopter due to inadequate airstrip infrastructure and challenging operating conditions, particularly during the rainy season. While this creates significant cost pressures, the service maintains operational efficiency through optimized routing, multi-stop scheduling, flexible fleet deployment, and a cost-recovery mechanism, while retaining the capacity to respond to emergencies.

The overall service is governed by the Steering Committee and User Group Committee, ensuring that operational decisions and resources remain responsive to the evolving needs of the humanitarian community.

Beyond service delivery, UNHAS strengthens the safety and longer-term sustainability of humanitarian aviation in the country through rigorous aviation safety and security standards, stakeholder coordination, capacity building, and infrastructure development.

items.title: DR Congo: Cluster Protection RDC : Aperçu des violations et abus des droits humains dans la province du Nord-Kivu, octobre 2026
items.author: Protection Cluster
items.content:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Protection Cluster

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

En octobre 2026, la situation de protection au Nord-Kivu est restée critique, marquée par une intensification des affrontements dans les territoires de Masisi, Walikale et Rutshuru. Cette situation se serait traduite par l’usage d’armes lourdes et de frappes de drone, des représailles contre les civils ainsi que des déplacements forcés.

FAITS SAILLANTS DE LA PÉRIODE

Intensification des hostilités : Des affrontements auraient opposé un groupe armé à une coalition de groupes armés dans les territoires de Masisi et de Walikale, et des frappes de drone auraient visé Binza (Rutshuru).

Déplacements forcés : Près de 2 580 ménages (environ 12 900 personnes) auraient été déplacés, dont 546 à Busanza (Rutshuru) et 450 à Kasake (Masisi).

Engins explosifs : Des projectiles tombés sur Kasake auraient fait 4 morts et 6 blessés, et des engins explosifs largués sur Kangati auraient tué 2 garçons.

Représailles et riposte Ebola : Des enlèvements contre rançon accompagnés de meurtres et des attaques de structures sanitaires à Butembo et Beni auraient été commis.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: Ukraine: Гуманітарна ситуація в Україні: оновлення оперативного реагування УВКБ ООН. 18 листопада 2026 р [UK]
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

ОПЕРАЦІЙНИЙ КОНТЕКСТ І ГОЛОВНІ ПОДІЇ:

• Упродовж жовтня Російська Федерація (РФ) і надалі здійснювала масовані обстріли із застосуванням засобів повітряного нападу в різних областях України. В умовах зниження температури повітря та наближення зимового періоду дедалі частіших ударів зазнавали об’єкти енергетичної та іншої критичної інфраструктури. Неодноразові обстріли спричиняли пошкодження об’єктів енергетичної інфраструктури й призводили до перебоїв в електро- й водопостачанні, а також у наданні інших життєво необхідних послуг. З наближенням холодного періоду через наслідки обстрілів підвищувалися ризики для мирних мешканців, зокрема для людей старшого віку й людей зі зниженою мобільністю. Як повідомляє Моніторингова місія ООН з прав людини, у жовтні 2026 р. щонайменше 372 цивільні особи загинули, а ще 1 981 – була поранена.

• Операції гуманітарної допомоги здійснюються в умовах загострення ситуації безпеки: у жовтні внаслідок щонайменше семи інцидентів у сфері безпеки під час реалізації програмних заходів УВКБ ООН постраждали організації-партнери Агентства. Йдеться, серед іншого, про обстріли, через які постраждали фахівці організацій-партнерів і їхня операційна діяльність, був пошкоджений гуманітарний транспорт і приміщення. Під неодноразовими ударами, зокрема, перебували проміжні пункти евакуації. Хоча інформації про загиблих пр ацівників УВКБ ООН або НУО – партнерів не надходило, подібні факти свідчать про нестабільність ситуації, за якої здійснюється операційна діяльність, і ризики для гуманітарних операцій.

• УВКБ ООН сприяло робочому візиту делегації Міністерства соціальної політики, сім’ї та єдності України до Женеви для участі у 77-й сесії Виконавчого комітету УВКБ ООН. Виступаючи на сесії Виконавчого комітету УВКБ ООН, очільник Міністерства, Денис Улютін, наголосив на важливості міжнародної гуманітарної підтримки України, захисту внутрішньо переміщених людей та інвестицій у довгострокові рішення.

• Програма реагування, втілювана УВКБ ООН на п’ятому році від початку повномасштабного російського вторгнення та на тринадцятому – від початку війни, покликана допомогти постраждалим від війни й внутрішньо переміщеним людям у пошуку сталих рішень, зокрема через адвокацію стратегічних змін у сфері житла й соціально-правового захисту.

items.title: Lebanon Quarterly Overview of RAIS Referrals - Q3 2026 · July – September
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Country: Lebanon
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

The Refugee Assistance Information System (RAIS) is a centralized inter-agency platform used by humanitarian actors to identify needs, coordinate referrals, and track responses at the individual level. By leveraging existing data and assistance records, it enables targeted referral pathways and supports broader monitoring, planning, and programming through analysis of evolving needs and trends. This dashboard presents referrals by participating actors (~600 users), offering key indicators and insights for coordinated, evidence-based decision-making, as part of the collective inter-agency effort, complementing referrals managed through other channels. Data should be interpreted in light of operational context, coverage, and reporting practices.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: Lebanon: RAIS Cumulative Assistance Summary – January to October 2026
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Country: Lebanon
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Find the RAIS assistance summary for January – October 2026, broken down by month, covering all organisations that reported into the system during this period. This is shared so each organisation can check what has been recorded against its name — month by month — and flag any corrections.

Missed reporting for a previous month? You can still back-report it in RAIS. Back-reported records will be included, so the figures will be correct in the next RAIS Assistance Report dashboard.

How to read this summary: each monthly column shows two figures. For in-kind and service assistance (CRI items, shelter kits and repairs, home visits, counselling), the top number is quantity distributed and the smaller number below is cases (no value shown). For cash-based assistance (Emergency Financial Assistance, EPCA, Protection Cash Assistance, MCAP, PCAP, ATM-credited cash, cash for food/education/shelter, NDA), the top number is cases and the smaller number below is value disbursed (USD). A dash (–) means no assistance of that type was reported by that organisation in that month.

A note on what "cases" means: the case figures in this summary are not unique beneficiaries. A "case" is a household or family that received assistance during that specific month. The same household may be counted more than once within this period — for example, if it received the same type of assistance in multiple months, or received different types of assistance (cash and/or in-kind) from the same organisation or from different organisations, during the same month or across different months. As a result, summing cases across months or across assistance types will overstate the number of distinct households reached.

items.creator: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.title: Lebanon: Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) - Midyear Report 2026
items.author: UN High Commissioner for Refugees
items.content:
Country: Lebanon
Sources: UN High Commissioner for Refugees, United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

The Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) Midyear Report 2026 presents an analysis of GBV incidents reported to 18 participating service providers across Lebanon between January and June 2026, comparing findings with the same period in 2025. The report examines trends in reported incidents, survivor profiles, displacement-related risks, access to services, and referral gaps against the backdrop of renewed hostilities, widespread displacement, and increasing humanitarian needs.

The report identifies a 32% decrease in reported GBV incidents compared with the first half of 2025. However, this decline should not be interpreted as a reduction in GBV prevalence. Conflict-related disruptions, reduced availability of services, funding constraints, displacement, and barriers to safe disclosure have affected survivors' ability to access assistance and report incidents.

Key findings include:

  • Women and girls accounted for 99% of reported survivors, while adults represented 92% of survivors.
  • Intimate partner violence (IPV) remained the predominant case context, accounting for 90% of reported incidents, with a 9% increase in reported IPV cases compared with midyear 2025.
  • Psychological/emotional abuse (39%) and physical assault (38%) were the most frequently reported forms of GBV.
  • Internally displaced persons accounted for 20% of reported survivors, highlighting the impact of renewed hostilities and displacement on protection risks and access to services.
  • Nearly one-third of survivors (29%) sought assistance more than one month after the incident, reflecting persistent barriers to timely reporting and support.
  • Significant service gaps remain, including limited access to specialized mental health services, with 52% of mental health referrals reported as unavailable, alongside gaps in livelihoods and recovery support.

The findings highlight how conflict, displacement, economic hardship, and reductions in humanitarian funding continue to affect GBV risks and survivors' access to essential services. The report calls for strengthened GBV risk mitigation in displacement settings, sustained survivor-centred case management and referral services, improved access to specialized mental health and economic recovery support, and greater investment in preventing and responding to intimate partner violence.

The report aims to inform evidence-based humanitarian programming, coordination, advocacy, and resource allocation to ensure continued access to safe, confidential, and quality GBV services across Lebanon.

Data limitation: GBVIMS findings reflect incidents reported by survivors who accessed participating service providers and consented to the anonymized use of their information. They do not represent the total number of GBV incidents or measure GBV prevalence in Lebanon.

items.creator: Action contre la Faim France
items.title: Burkina Faso: Production de biomasse en 2026 - Analyses et perspectives pour 2027
items.author: Action contre la Faim France
items.content:
Countries: Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal
Source: Action contre la Faim France

Please refer to the attached file.

FAITS SAILLANTS

• Production nationale de biomasse légèrement supérieure à la moyenne historique, avec une anomalie de +0,5σ, soit 104 % de la normale.

• Net recul des productions par rapport aux années exceptionnelles de 2022, 2024 et 2025.

• Situation moins favorable qu’en 2025, marquée par d’importantes disparités spatiales.

• Excédents importants dans plusieurs provinces de l’est, notamment le Koulpélogo, le Gourma, la Komandjari et le Yagha.

• Production inférieure à la moyenne dans plusieurs provinces du centre et de l’ouest, particulièrement dans le Bassitenga, le Ganzourgou, la Sissili, le Balé, et le Mouhoun.

• Vulnérabilité liée à la biomasse globalement proche de la normale à l’échelle nationale, mais présence de poches de vulnérabilité nécessitant une surveillance.

• Les contraintes sécuritaires et de mobilité continuent de limiter l’accès à certaines ressources pastorales.

INTRODUCTION

Ce document présente une évaluation de la production de biomasse végétale au cours de la saison des pluies 2026 au Burkina Faso. L’analyse repose sur les indicateurs satellitaires de production de biomasse, d’anomalie par rapport à la moyenne historique et de vulnérabilité, complétés par l’analyse des variations saisonnières et interannuelles. À l’échelle nationale, la production de biomasse de 2026 est légèrement supérieure à la moyenne historique, avec une anomalie de +0,5σ, correspondant à 104 % de la normale. Cette situation demeure toutefois sensiblement moins favorable que celle observée en 2025 et masque d’importantes disparités territoriales. Plusieurs provinces de l’est et du sud-est du pays présentent des excédents marqués, tandis que des déficits apparaissent dans différentes zones du centre et de l’ouest. Cette hétérogénéité implique d’apprécier la situation pastorale à une échelle locale. Au-delà de la quantité de biomasse disponible, son accessibilité constitue un facteur déterminant, notamment dans les zones affectées par l’insécurité, les restrictions de mobilité et la concentration du cheptel. Le suivi des zones déficitaires ou soumises à une forte pression pastorale reste donc nécessaire à l’approche de la soudure 2027.
